clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant ataxia caused by an intronic GGCCTG hexanucleotide repeat expansion in NOP56, first characterised in Japanese (Asidan) and Galician (Costa da Morte) populations
Typical onset is in mid-to-late adulthood with slowly progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and a tremor-ataxia picture

A distinguishing feature is later development of motor neuron signs, notably tongue atrophy and fasciculations, with limb fasciculations and hyperreflexia, giving a cerebellar-plus lower-motor-neuron phenotype
Sensorineural hearing loss is a recognised associated feature and can help point towards the diagnosis
Brain MRI shows cerebellar atrophy, initially vermian, with later brainstem and cerebral atrophy as disease advances
Diagnosis requires repeat-primed PCR or equivalent to detect the NOP56 expansion, as it is missed by standard exome and small-panel sequencing
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, including physiotherapy, speech and swallow support, hearing rehabilitation and surveillance for aspiration risk
reference.pathophysiology: SCA36 is caused by an expanded GGCCTG hexanucleotide repeat in the first intron of NOP56, a gene encoding a nucleolar protein involved in ribosomal RNA processing. The expansion is thought to act largely through a toxic RNA gain-of-function mechanism, in which repeat-containing transcripts form nuclear foci that sequester RNA-binding proteins and disturb RNA metabolism, alongside possible reduction of NOP56 expression. Purkinje cells and brainstem motor neurons are particularly vulnerable, producing the combination of progressive cerebellar degeneration and lower motor neuron loss that characterises the disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 35 and TGM6-related tremor-ataxia
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis when motor neuron signs dominate
Kennedy disease (spinobulbar muscular atrophy) with bulbar and lower motor neuron features
additionalInvestigations: Repeat-primed PCR (or Southern blot) for the NOP56 hexanucleotide expansion
Brain MRI to characterise the pattern and progression of cerebellar and brainstem atrophy
Audiometry to detect associated sensorineural hearing loss
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to document motor neuron involvement
Exclusion of common repeat-expansion SCAs before or alongside NOP56 testing
Detailed pedigree analysis to confirm dominant transmission and population origin
redFlags: Rapidly progressive bulbar weakness with dysphagia and aspiration risk
Respiratory compromise from advancing motor neuron involvement
Marked weight loss and malnutrition secondary to swallowing difficulty
Recurrent falls with injury as gait ataxia worsens
reference.prognosis: SCA36 progresses slowly, often over one to two decades, with gait and speech becoming increasingly affected; the later addition of motor neuron features and bulbar involvement contributes to disability and can shorten survival through aspiration and respiratory complications. Many patients remain ambulant for years before requiring aids.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because the intronic repeat expansion is not detected by exome or standard gene panels
Misdiagnosing the disorder as motor neuron disease when lower motor neuron signs appear before ataxia is recognised
Overlooking associated hearing loss, which is a useful diagnostic clue
Failing to arrange swallow assessment despite emerging bulbar signs
Not providing genetic counselling for at-risk relatives given dominant inheritance
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
